paras: The Perry County Ku-Klux threats and Perryville newspaper fire were a campaign of death threats, arson and armed intimidation at Perryville, Arkansas, in May and June 1881 against County Judge L. M. Harris, editor John L. Matthews and others by a group signing itself the "regular organized Ku-Klux." On a Sunday night, June 5 by the first dispatches, the newspaper office was set on fire; citizens put out the flames. Harris and Matthews fled before armed men came asking for them, and Governor Churchill sent General R. C. Newton to investigate. Matthews was shot dead outside his office in July in what dispatches called the same troubles.

The Little Rock Democrat described Perryville, the county seat, as a town of saloons without churches or schools until Harris became county judge and a new newspaper backed "law and order." A Gazette special from Morrilton traced the threats to prosecutions begun by Harris and published by Matthews; Harris blamed his efforts to make two delinquent sheriffs settle with the county. The Memphis Public Ledger named the accused defaulting deputy sheriffs as George Myers and James Isham, whose attorneys suggested Harris resign or leave. A later Gazette account added that Harris's opponents claimed Matthews had influenced "objectionable proceedings" in his court.

On May 25, the Gazette special said, Harris and Matthews each got a notice through the Perryville post office to leave the county within fifteen days or be killed by the "Regular organized Ku Klux." The letter to Harris warned that he would "go like Mathews damed old printing office" and promised "fire and gunpowder"; other prominent citizens received similar warnings.

Little Rock dispatches of June 6 reported that the office had been fired at midnight the previous Sunday and that citizens put out the flames and drove the incendiaries away. The Gazette special dated the fire to May 30. The deadline passed on June 8, a day after Harris and Matthews left; at one o'clock the next morning a body of armed men rode in and asked for them. A later Gazette account put the party at about twenty men and said Matthews met them on the square, where they rode away without speaking to him. The Public Ledger added that the county assessor and two other residents were "very roughly handled," threatened with death and driven out.

Harris reached Little Rock on June 9, and Churchill sent Newton to Perryville as his messenger, accompanied by Harris. Two men named Peyton and McGee were reported arrested on a charge of firing the Times office; no report of a trial was found.

About nine o'clock on the night of July 21, Matthews was shot as he returned from a well to his office; eighteen buckshot struck his left side and arm, and he died. The gunman ran off unidentified, and a notice was left at Harris's residence telling him to leave the county. On July 30, with justices reported afraid to issue writs, Churchill sent Newton into the county with the Quapaw Guards, a step dispatches called martial law.

The first reports, from Little Rock on June 6, ran as "Ku-Klux in Arkansas," "Ku-Klux Outrages" and "Outlawry in Arkansas" in Washington, Chicago and New York dailies. Several printed it beside an unrelated note on mustering the "colored" Neel Guards of Pine Bluff; the Perryville reports gave no race for the threatened men or the band. Copies circulated into mid-June with errors that put the town in "Berry county" or in Kansas.

The Little Rock Democrat, reprinted as "Cowardly Attempt" in the Osceola Times, urged the authorities to "rid the county of the band of rascals." A later Democrat correspondent, quoted by the Russellville Democrat, called the Ku-Klux "probably a myth." Of Matthews's killing, the Chicago Tribune said it was "the result of Ku-Klux troubles," while the Gazette's Morrilton correspondent called it "a feud without political significance."

Whether a band existed was disputed: the Russellville Democrat said there were "two sides" and that the alleged Ku-Klux offered to help the sheriff, and some citizens later called the riders deer hunters. The fire's date varies between the Sunday before June 6 and May 30, and the Little Rock Democrat said the newspaper had been attacked repeatedly.

reader.title: Perry County Ku-Klux threats and Perryville newspaper fire
bases: A band signing itself the 'regular organized Ku-Klux' mailed notices ordering a judge, an editor and others to leave the county on pain of death, fired the newspaper office and rode into town armed to look for them (A1, A10, A14, A28).

Independent Little Rock and Morrilton specials agree on the death notices, the newspaper-office fire and the armed visit (A1, A2, A10, A14), but a Little Rock Democrat correspondent called the Ku-Klux 'probably a myth' and the trouble 'greatly exaggerated' (A19), and citizens later called the armed men deer hunters (A28).

accounts.label: Little Rock wire (June 6)
accounts.gist: Ku-Klux were driving people from Perry County with threatening letters and tried to burn Perryville by firing the newspaper office on Sunday night; citizens put out the fire and vowed to bring the outlaws to justice.

accounts.label: Gazette's Morrilton special (June 9)
accounts.gist: Harris and Matthews got death notices on May 25, left before the deadline, and armed men came looking for them at 1 a.m.; the trouble arose from Harris's prosecutions, and the Times office was fired on May 30.

accounts.label: Judge Harris
accounts.gist: Harris blamed his efforts to compel two delinquent sheriffs to settle with the county and feared the Times office had been destroyed and lives lost.

accounts.label: Little Rock Democrat correspondent
accounts.gist: Found little excitement at Perryville, called the trouble greatly exaggerated and the Ku-Klux probably a myth, and said the alleged Ku-Klux offered to help the sheriff.

accounts.label: Gazette special (July 22)
accounts.gist: About twenty armed men had ridden in on the deadline; some citizens said they were deer hunters; Matthews was shot from the dark by an unseen man, and the killing was regarded as a feud without political significance.

framing.detail: National and Southern dailies ran the Little Rock wire under 'Ku-Klux in Arkansas', 'Ku-Klux Outrages' and 'Outlawry in Arkansas', calling the band 'outlaws'.
The Little Rock Democrat, reprinted as 'Cowardly Attempt', praised Harris and the paper and urged authorities to 'rid the county of the band of rascals'.
The Russellville Democrat said there were 'two sides' and printed a view that the Ku-Klux was a myth got up by 'a few schemers'.
Reports of Matthews's death called it a 'cowardly assassination' and the county a 'reign of terror'.
